nameStory: Evening Stock gets its evocative name from its magical nighttime behavior - while its flowers may look unremarkable during the day, they release an intensely sweet, intoxicating fragrance as evening falls. This enchanting perfume is designed to attract night-flying moths for pollination, making twilight garden walks an aromatic adventure.
description: Evening Stock is a delicate annual flowering plant that belongs to the mustard family, though you'd never guess it from its sweet fragrance! This slender plant grows 1-2 feet tall with narrow, grayish-green leaves and small four-petaled flowers that open in shades of pink, purple, or white. Originally from the Mediterranean region, it's grown as an ornamental garden plant and occasionally escapes cultivation in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small four-petaled flowers in pink, purple, or white that may look wilted during the day but perk up and release an incredibly sweet, honey-like fragrance at dusk

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves with a soft, slightly fuzzy texture and grayish-green color that feel velvety when rubbed gently

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright annual plant reaching 1-2 feet tall with a somewhat scraggly, open branching pattern

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed pods (siliques) typical of the mustard family, splitting open when mature to reveal small seeds

habitat: Evening Stock is primarily found in cultivated gardens and occasionally escapes to disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, or garden edges. It prefers well-drained, sandy or loamy soils in full sun to partial shade. Being a Mediterranean native, it thrives in areas with good drainage and doesn't tolerate wet, heavy soils.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants develop their characteristic narrow, grayish leaves in a small rosette.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom from mid to late summer, with the magical evening fragrance becoming most noticeable during warm, still nights.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open, releasing seeds for next year's plants before the first frost kills the annual plant.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible, as this annual plant completes its life cycle in one growing season.

funFact: Evening Stock's flowers are essentially solar-powered perfume factories - they close up and become nearly scentless during the hot daytime hours to conserve their precious fragrant oils, then open wide at dusk and pump out their intoxicating scent so powerfully that a small patch can perfume an entire garden!
confusionNotes: Evening Stock might be confused with other small mustard family flowers, but no other plant in New England has that distinctive evening fragrance combined with four-petaled flowers. Remember: if it smells absolutely divine at dusk, you've found your Evening Stock!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name including 'Stock,' Evening Stock is quite different from the more familiar Garden Stock (Matthiola incana) that florists use - Evening Stock is much more delicate and temporary, grown specifically for its nighttime fragrance rather than showy daytime blooms.
compareHints: Evening Stock is the only member of the Stock genus commonly found in New England gardens. Compared to other mustard family plants in the region, it's much more delicate and fragrant than robust species like garlic mustard or winter cress. Unlike its mustard cousins that often have a sharp, peppery smell when crushed, Evening Stock's leaves have little scent - all the perfume is saved for the flowers at nightfall.
